The Tagus River. The Iberian Peninsula's longest river, flowing six hundred and forty-five miles from central Spain through Portugal to the Atlantic Ocean. It forms a natural boundary between central Spain and Estremadura, and its estuary at Lisbon is one of Europe's finest harbors, making it central to Portuguese maritime power.

The Tagus is the longest river of the Iberian Peninsula. It originates in the mountains of central Spain and flows generally westward toward the Atlantic. It forms a dramatic gorge in the Montes de Toledo region of Spain, historically difficult to cross, making it a natural defensive line. The Tagus estuary at Lisbon provides a deep natural harbor that enabled Portugal's Age of Discovery maritime expansion, allowing Portuguese explorers to venture forth across the oceans.

The river serves as part of the Spain-Portugal border in some reaches, though water-sharing rights between the two countries remain politically sensitive even today. Tidal influence extends far inland, and Lisbon's position at the estuary's mouth made it a crucial port for Phoenician, Roman, and medieval traders. The Salazar Dam, also called the Barragem do Salazar, is one of Europe's largest dams, creating a massive reservoir for hydropower and irrigation.

The Tagus originates in Spanish territory and forms major geographical features of central Spain. The estuary dominates Lisbon's geography and Portugal's entire relationship with Atlantic trade and European commerce. The river's harbor was instrumental to Portuguese maritime exploration and colonialism, enabling the Portuguese empire to expand its influence across the world. The Tagus is one of the Iberian Peninsula's most defining geographical features.
